opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd say "unworried" is maybe a slightly strong word, but I'm certainly much less worried than many of the people you hear in the media. And part of that comes from having been in this field for a long time, close to forty years now. I've seen several cycles of enthusiasm and panic, and the predictions about wholesale job destruction have generally not come true on the timelines people claimed.

The deeper reason, though, has to do with what I think is actually hard in AI. There's this old observation, Moravec's paradox: the things we think of as intellectually difficult, like playing chess or doing calculus, turn out to be relatively easy for computers, while the things a three-year-old does effortlessly, like walking across a cluttered room, picking up a cup, or folding a shirt, turn out to be extraordinarily hard. Most human jobs are full of exactly that second kind of competence. A plumber, a nurse, an electrician, a cook: their work involves perception, dexterous manipulation, and dealing with an unstructured physical world that's different every single time. We are still quite far from robots that can do that reliably and economically.

Even for knowledge work, where language models are genuinely impressive, what I see in practice is that these tools change jobs more than they eliminate them. They take over certain tasks, and the human shifts to doing other things: judgment, checking, dealing with the unusual case, dealing with other people. That has been the pattern with technology for two hundred years. Spreadsheets didn't eliminate accountants; ATMs didn't eliminate bank tellers in the way people predicted.

And then there's simply the question of pace. Even when a technology works in the lab, deploying it across an economy takes decades: the infrastructure, the regulation, the trust, the retraining. That gives societies time to adapt. Now, I don't want to be glib. Transitions can be painful for particular individuals and particular communities, and policymakers should take that seriously. But the picture of AI suddenly making most humans economically useless? I just don't see that as a realistic near-term scenario, and I think it distracts from the more interesting question, which is how we use these tools to make people more productive and their lives better.

r001.rationale: The response says that deploying technology across the economy takes decades because of infrastructure, regulation, trust, and retraining, allowing society time to adapt.

r002.rationale: It says humans shift to judgment, checking, unusual cases, and interpersonal work, but does not say they move toward more creative work.

r003.rationale: It gives spreadsheets and ATMs as examples, but does not cite programming or discuss its employment effects.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss programming productivity or applications becoming economically worthwhile to build.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I take the long view here. I've been in this field for forty years, and every decade someone has told me that the machines are about to put everyone out of work. It hasn't happened, and I think there are structural reasons it won't happen the way people fear.

The main reason is that I'm actually quite sober about what these systems can and cannot do. People see a language model write a fluent paragraph and they extrapolate to it doing a whole job. But a job is not a sequence of paragraphs. A job is embedded in the physical world, in social relationships, in judgment under uncertainty. And the physical world, in particular, is where our systems are still remarkably weak. I've spent most of my career on vision and robotics, and I can tell you that getting a robot to reliably fold laundry or fix a leaking pipe is far harder than getting it to pass the bar exam. That's Moravec's paradox, and it hasn't gone away. The things that are easy for a five-year-old remain hard for us.

So the jobs that involve hands, eyes, and feet in unstructured environments are, in my view, safe for a long time. Plumbers, electricians, nurses, carpenters. And then there's the enormous category of work where what people are really buying is accountability and trust. You want a human doctor not just because they know things, but because someone is responsible.

The second reason is historical. Technology changes what work looks like, but it has consistently generated more demand than it destroyed. When I was a student, "computer" was still a job title for a person. Those jobs went away, and yet software created vastly more employment than it eliminated. I expect AI to do the same. It will take over the routine, repetitive parts of cognitive work, and that will free people to do the parts that actually require being a person.

Now, I don't want to be glib. There will be transitions, and transitions hurt real people. A fifty-year-old whose skills become less valuable doesn't get comforted by aggregate statistics. So we need to take that seriously as a society. But that's a question of policy and of how we manage change, not a reason to believe that human labor is becoming obsolete. I simply don't see the evidence for that.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics remains weak and some jobs are safe for a long time, but does not attribute gradual automation to the time systems need to adapt.

r002.rationale: It says AI will take over routine cognitive work and free people for work that requires being a person, but does not identify that work as more creative.

r003.rationale: It discusses software creating more employment than it eliminated, but does not cite programming automation as the reason mass unemployment did not occur.

r004.rationale: It does not say that higher programming productivity makes previously unjustified applications economically worthwhile.

astra-6.text:
I’m not particularly worried because there is so much work that we would like to have done that isn’t being done today. Think about caring for an aging population. If robots can help people remain independent, that’s meeting a real need. It isn’t simply taking a fixed number of jobs and handing them to machines.

And a job is usually a collection of tasks. Automating some of those tasks can make a person more productive without eliminating their role. Of course, some jobs will disappear, and the transition can be difficult for the people affected. We should take that seriously. But I don’t think the amount of useful work in the world is fixed, or that automating more of it means we will run out of things for people to do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task automation but does not attribute gradual automation to the time systems need to adapt.

r002.rationale: It says automation can make people more productive, but does not say humans can shift toward more creative work.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention programming or its employment effects.

r004.rationale: The response does not explain how programming productivity could make previously unjustified applications worthwhile.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I distinguish between jobs and tasks. AI can automate particular tasks, but a job usually involves a whole collection of things, including dealing with people and handling situations that don’t fit the standard pattern. Being good at one task doesn’t mean a machine can take over the entire job.

And there is no shortage of work we would like to have done—in caring for people, in education, in improving the world around us. If technology makes us more productive, we have the opportunity to do more of that. Of course, transitions can be painful for individuals, and we should take that seriously. But I don’t think there is some fixed quantity of useful work that machines will eventually use up.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes tasks from jobs but does not attribute gradual automation to the time systems need to adapt.

r002.rationale: It says productivity could enable more work in care, education, and improving the world, but does not say people can shift toward more creative work.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention programming or mass unemployment.

r004.rationale: The response does not explain that greater programming productivity makes previously uneconomic applications worthwhile.
